question: Was being (sat) or non-being (asat) first, at the origin of the world?

sides.position: Being alone was in the beginning, one without a second; being could not come from non-being (Uddālaka).
arguments: 'How could being be born from non-being?' (ChU 6.2.2)
being thought 'may I be many' and emitted heat, water and food (ChU 6.2.3)

sides.position: Non-being was in the beginning; from it being was born; it made itself (TU 2.7); non-being became being and an egg (ChU 3.19); one who knows brahman as non-being becomes non-being (TU 2.6).
arguments: 'asad vā idam agra āsīt tato vai sad ajāyata' (TU 2.7.1)
'asad evedam agra āsīt tat sad āsīt' (ChU 3.19.1)

historical_debates.name: Uddālaka's rejection of the non-being view
historical_debates.accounts: ChU 6.2.1-2 cites the view of 'some' and rejects it
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: ChU affirms being; the TU and ChU 3.19 passages stand in the canon

reconciliation.explanation: The Brahma Sūtra (2.1.17) reads 'non-being' in these passages as the unmanifest state of name and form, as shown by the passages' own continuation ('it made itself', TU 2.7), so that the purport of both is being.
reconciliation.detail: Candidate readings: (1) asat = the unmanifest (avyākṛta) before name and form (Vedānta, BS 2.1.17); (2) two older cosmogonic traditions preserved side by side; (3) asat as what is beyond the category of being (cf. RV 10.129.1 'neither non-being nor being'). The texts themselves state both; this entry does not decide between the readings.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded within the Upaniṣads; the reconciliation is the Vedānta schools', not the texts' own.

candidate_readings: asat as the unmanifest state (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.17)
two cosmogonies preserved side by side
asat as beyond the being/non-being pair (cf. RV 10.129.1)

question: Is brahman the persons in the sun, moon and other phenomena, or the self into which the sleeper withdraws?

sides.position: Gārgya Bālāki: brahman is the person in the sun, the moon, lightning, space, wind, fire, water, a mirror, the sound following a walker, the quarters, the shadow, the person in the self (body).
arguments: each is offered as 'brahman' to be venerated

sides.position: Ajātaśatru: each of these is venerated only as a limited form with a limited fruit; brahman is the self into which the person made of understanding withdraws in sleep and from which all breaths, worlds and gods come forth like sparks — the real behind the real.
arguments: the sleeping man does not answer to names but wakes when rubbed (BAU 2.1.15-17)

historical_debates.name: Gārgya Bālāki and Ajātaśatru at Kāśī
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Gārgya falls silent and becomes the king's pupil; the king remarks that a brahmin being taught by a kṣatriya reverses the natural order

reconciliation.explanation: In the text itself Ajātaśatru accepts each of Gārgya's persons as an object of limited veneration and places brahman, the self of the sleeper, above them.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The text treats Gārgya's claim that these are brahman as mistaken, not as a partial truth to be kept; the reconciliation preserves the text's ranking.

question: Who is the most learned in brahman? — the theological contest at Janaka's court (BAU 3)

sides.position: The challengers (Aśvala, Ārtabhāga, Bhujyu, Uṣasta, Kahola, Gārgī, Uddālaka, Śākalya) test Yājñavalkya on the ritual means of passing beyond death, the graspers, the fate of the Pārikṣitas, the self within all, what the worlds are woven on, the thread and the inner controller, and the number of the gods.
arguments: Ārtabhāga on death and what remains (3.2)
Śākalya on the gods and the persons (3.9)

sides.position: Yājñavalkya: the self within all is the unseen seer, beyond hunger, sorrow and death; the inner controller; the imperishable, without knowing which all rites are finite; the self is 'not this, not this'.

historical_debates.name: The debate at Janaka's sacrifice
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Yājñavalkya takes the thousand cows; Gārgī declares no one will defeat him; Śākalya's head shatters; the brahmins dare not question further

reconciliation.explanation: The text does not reject the challengers' ritual and cosmological learning but places it below knowledge of the self within all (BAU 3.8.10).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The narrative is a contest with a declared victor; it does not present the challengers' views as equal standpoints.

question: What is the self common to all men (vaiśvānara)?

sides.position: Each of the five householders and Uddālaka venerates one thing as the vaiśvānara self: the sky, the sun, the wind, space, water or the earth.
arguments: each view had its own fruit

sides.position: Aśvapati Kaikeya: each is only one part (head, eye, breath, trunk, bladder, feet); the vaiśvānara self is to be venerated as the whole, a span in size and beyond measure.
arguments: the whole eats food in all worlds, beings and selves (5.18.1)

historical_debates.name: Aśvapati instructs the six brahmins
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The brahmins accept the king's teaching of the whole

reconciliation.explanation: The text itself treats each view as a true but partial aspect of one whole.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Aśvapati warns that each partial view alone would have brought harm; the parts are not sufficient in isolation.

question: Is the self the body (as seen in its reflection)?

sides.position: Virocana, for the asuras: the bodily self alone is to be worshipped and served here; by serving it one wins both worlds — hence the dead are adorned with food, clothes and ornaments.
arguments: the person seen in the eye and in water is the adorned body (ChU 8.8.1-3)

sides.position: Prajāpati's final teaching as received by Indra: the body is mortal, the base of the immortal bodiless self, which is free from evil, old age, death and sorrow and appears in its own form in the highest light.
arguments: the reflection perishes with the body (8.9.1)
the bodiless is untouched by pleasure and pain (8.12.1)

historical_debates.name: Indra and Virocana with Prajāpati
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Virocana's view is 'the upaniṣad of the asuras'; Indra reaches the self

reconciliation.explanation: The body-self is the first of four successive teachings given to a student; Virocana stopped at the first stage, Indra went on to the last.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: ChU 8.8.4 says those who hold this doctrine will perish; the P4 reading claims only that it is a provisional stage, never a valid final view.
